transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?

Well, my wife actually made the appointment. She's been on me about it for a while. What finally made me agree to come in, I guess, is that I just don't care about the things that used to keep me balanced. You know, I used to do these weekend sailing races. It's funny, actually, the last time I was out on the water, the wind died completely right in the middle of a tack, just dead calm. We sat there for two hours baking in the sun. My buddy Dave was furious, but I usually love that kind of thing, just being out there. But now... I don't know, even that sounds exhausting. Same with my Saturday historical society shift. I used to love cataloging the old maps—did you know our town was originally planned with a radial street grid before they scrapped it in the 1890s? Fascinating stuff. But lately, going there feels like a chore I keep putting off. Even tinkering in my woodshop... I just look at my tools and walk away. I just can't be bothered.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, lately?

Down? Um... no, I wouldn't say depressed. Not like crying or sad all day, if that's what you mean. I still get up and log in for work. Actually, work has been... well, we just transitioned to this new project management software at the firm. It's supposed to streamline our deliverables, but honestly, it's just created so many more meetings. My director, Greg, he insisted on having this daily alignment call at 8 AM sharp. 8 AM! And half our vendor team is out in Seattle, so they're having to dial in at 5 AM their time. It's completely ridiculous. I tried explaining to him that we need to respect the time zones if we want good vendor relations, but he's on this whole "win the morning" kick because he read some book by a tech CEO last month. He even bought hardcover copies for the whole office and left them on our desks. 

Anyway... what did you ask me? Oh, right, feeling down. No, I don't think I'm depressed like that. Just... like I was saying with the sailing and the woodshop. I just don't have the energy to care about it.
Have you found that you don’t enjoy or look forward to things that used to bring you pleasure, even when you do them?

Yeah, exactly. That's what I was trying to say before about the sailing and the historical society. I just don't care about them anymore. Like, last Sunday, I actually forced myself to go out to the woodshop to try and snap out of it. I was supposed to be finishing this... well, it's a mid-century modern inspired bird feeder. I actually saw the blueprints for it in a magazine at my dentist's office. 

Dr. Aris, my dentist, he just remodeled his whole waiting room and put in this massive saltwater aquarium. It's really beautiful, but he was telling me it costs an absolute fortune to maintain because of the live coral. You have to keep the pH levels perfectly balanced or the whole ecosystem just crashes, which honestly sounds like a project management nightmare if you ask me. I told him he should really track the maintenance schedule on a Gantt chart, just to visualize the dependencies, but he looked at me like I was crazy. 

But anyway, where was I? Oh, the woodshop. Right. So I went out there, stood at my workbench, picked up my tools, and just... nothing. No spark. Even though I was right there ready to do it, it just felt like another chore on my to-do list that I couldn't be bothered with. I just put everything down and walked right back inside.
Have you been feeling tired or having little energy most days, even if you’re not doing much?

Tired? No, I wouldn't say I'm physically tired. I have enough energy, I guess. I mean, I'm still getting up and doing my job. Speaking of my job, you wouldn't believe the energy Greg expects us to have. He's actually talking about organizing a company retreat now. A retreat! He wants us to go to this ropes course out in the woods somewhere. He says it's going to build trust and synergy. Synergy! I haven't heard anyone use that word seriously since the late nineties. 

I remember back in '98, I was working for this logistics firm, and they brought in this consultant who just kept repeating "synergy" and "paradigm shift." He wore these ridiculous suspenders, bright red, with little dollar signs on them. Can you imagine? He actually made us sit in a circle and pass around a talking stick. A literal stick he picked up in the parking lot. 

So no, I'm not really tired or lacking energy. I'm just... not interested in doing the things I used to do.
Have you been feeling this way—losing interest in things you used to enjoy—for at least two weeks straight?

Two weeks? Oh, gosh, no. It's been way longer than that. This whole... whatever you want to call it, this lack of interest, it's been going on since the scaffolding accident during the business readjustment. That was a little over a year ago now. 

You know, that readjustment was supposed to be this huge step forward for the firm. They brought in all these contractors to remodel the office space to make it "open concept." They tore down all the cubicles. I had a corner cubicle, actually, right by the window. I had this great view of the old oak tree in the parking lot. There was this family of squirrels living in it, and I used to watch them hoarding acorns in the fall. It was fascinating, really, seeing how systematic they were about it. Like little furry project managers. 

But then they tore the walls down, and suddenly I'm sitting at this long communal table with six other people, and I can hear every time Susan from accounting chews her gum. She always chews peppermint, the really strong kind, and she snaps it. Snap, snap, snap, all day long. I tried bringing in noise-canceling headphones, the really expensive ones with the active EQ, but Greg said they weren't "conducive to a collaborative environment." 

But yeah, the accident happened right in the middle of all that construction. So it's been over a year since I've really cared about my hobbies.
Have you been feeling like you're not worth much or feeling guilty about things you've done or not done lately?

Guilty? Yeah, I guess you could say that. There's just this... this low-grade dread and guilt that kind of follows me around everywhere now. It's like this heavy feeling that I should have seen one more risk coming with that whole project, even though people keep telling me all the standard controls were in place. 

Speaking of controls, you wouldn't believe the lack of quality control at the dry cleaners down the street. I took my good wool suit there—the charcoal gray one I bought for my cousin's wedding three years ago. Beautiful suit, Italian wool. Anyway, I get it back, and they've completely pressed the lapels flat. Just ruined the roll of the lapel. I tried explaining to the kid at the counter about how the canvas interlining needs to be steamed, not pressed, but he just stared at me blankly. He was wearing this t-shirt with a cartoon avocado on it that said "Let's Guac and Roll." I mean, who wears that to work? 

So I had to take the suit to this old tailor across town, Mr. Rossi. He's been there for forty years, tiny little shop that smells like chalk and old steam. He took one look at it and just shook his head. He's a true craftsman, you know? He actually uses a heavy iron and a tailor's clapper to set the seams. It's a dying art. 

But yeah, the guilt. It's just always there, like I missed something obvious on the risk register, even when everyone says I didn't.
Have you noticed that you're having trouble thinking clearly, making decisions, or focusing on tasks lately?

Trouble thinking clearly? No, I wouldn't say that. My focus is fine, honestly. I'm still managing all my projects at work without any issues. Actually, speaking of focus, you should see the new project management software Greg is trying to force us to use. It's an absolute nightmare. It's supposed to "streamline our workflow," but it's just this convoluted mess of color-coded tags and Kanban boards. 

I spent three hours yesterday just trying to figure out how to assign a sub-task to a different department. Three hours! And the interface is this blinding, stark white with neon accents. It gives me a headache just looking at it. I told Greg we should just stick with the old system. Sure, it was a little clunky, and it crashed if you tried to export a report larger than fifty pages, but at least we all knew how to use it. 

I remember when we first got that old system, back in 2012. We had this trainer come in, this woman named Brenda. She had the most incredible collection of novelty brooches. Every day was a different one—a rhinestone poodle, a miniature teapot, a little enameled frog. I asked her about them once, and she told me she scours estate sales on the weekends just to find them. She had this whole elaborate filing system for them at home, categorized by theme and era. 

But anyway, no, my concentration is perfectly fine. I don't have any trouble making decisions or anything like that.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight lately, like eating a lot more or a lot less than usual?

Appetite? Weight? No, not really. I mean, I eat about the same as I always have. My weight hasn't really fluctuated much since my thirties. I try to stick to a routine, you know? Oatmeal in the morning, a sandwich for lunch. 

Speaking of sandwiches, they just opened this new deli near the office. It's one of those artisanal places where they charge you fifteen dollars for a turkey club. But I will say, they make their own sourdough bread in-house. You can smell it baking if you walk by around ten in the morning. It's a fantastic smell, really yeasty and sharp. I was talking to the baker—this guy with a massive beard and tattoos all up his arms—and he was telling me about their sourdough starter. Apparently, it's over forty years old. They call it "The Mother." They have to feed it every single day, like a pet. He said if the temperature in the kitchen drops even a few degrees, the whole batch of dough can be ruined. 

It made me think about my aunt Clara. She used to bake bread, but she never used a starter. She just bought those little packets of active dry yeast from the grocery store. The ones with the little red spoon on the front. She kept them in a tin box in the pantry, right next to her collection of loose-leaf teas. She had this one tea, I think it was Earl Grey, but it had these dried blue cornflower petals mixed into it. It looked so pretty in the jar. 

But yeah, my appetite is totally normal. No changes there.
Have you noticed that you've been moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or on the contrary, that you can't sit still and feel restless?

Moving slower or feeling restless? Um, no, I don't think so. I feel like my energy levels and how I move around are pretty much the same as always. I'm not pacing the halls or anything. 

Though, talking about moving slowly, you should see the traffic on I-95 during the morning commute lately. It is just a parking lot. I sat there for forty-five minutes yesterday just trying to get past the exit for the mall. And they're doing all this construction on the overpass, right? They've got those giant concrete barriers set up, the ones with the little orange flashing lights on top. 

I was watching this one construction worker while I was stuck there. He was operating one of those massive excavators, the really big yellow ones. It's amazing how precise they can be with those huge metal buckets. He was picking up these large chunks of concrete and placing them into a dump truck, just so gently, like he was handling eggshells. It reminded me of my neighbor's kid, Tommy. He's got this entire sandbox in his backyard dedicated to toy construction equipment. Tonka trucks, mostly. The old metal ones, not the cheap plastic ones they make now. His dad actually went on eBay and bought a bunch of vintage ones from the seventies. They weigh a ton, and the paint is all chipped, but they're practically indestructible. 

But anyway, no, I haven't noticed any changes in my own movements. I'm definitely not restless or slowed down.
Have you ever felt this way before—like you’ve lost interest in the things you used to enjoy—for a period of two weeks or longer?

Lost interest? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I still like doing the things I usually do. Like I said, I still enjoy my routine and going to work, even with Greg's terrible new software. 

Speaking of software, did you know that the first computer bug was an actual bug? A moth, I think. It got stuck in a relay of the Harvard Mark II computer back in the 1940s. Grace Hopper was the one who found it. She taped it into the logbook. I saw a picture of that logbook once in a documentary. It was this thick, leather-bound book, and the pages were all yellowed and brittle-looking. 

My grandfather had a book like that. It was his ledger from when he ran a hardware store in the sixties. He kept track of everything by hand. Every nail, every hammer, every can of paint. He had this beautiful, looping cursive handwriting. You don't see handwriting like that anymore. Now everyone just types or texts. My nephew, he's fourteen, and I swear his thumbs move faster than I can even process. He was showing me this game he plays on his phone, something with building blocks and zombies. I couldn't make heads or tails of it, but he was completely engrossed. 

But no, to answer your question, I haven't had any periods where I just lost interest in things for weeks at a time. Nothing like that.
Have you ever had a period in your life when you felt down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks in a row?

Down or depressed? For two weeks? No, I can't say I've ever really had a time like that. I mean, sure, everyone gets bummed out for a day or two, but not for weeks on end. 

Though, you know what really gets people down? The weather we've been having. It's been raining for, what, five days straight? It's that misty, drizzly kind of rain, too, where an umbrella doesn't even help because it just blows right under it. My neighbor across the street—Mr. Henderson, he's retired, used to be a postal worker—he has this immaculate lawn. I mean, it looks like a golf course. He's out there every weekend with an edger, making sure the lines along the sidewalk are perfectly straight. But with all this rain, his yard is turning into a swamp. I saw him out there yesterday in these bright yellow rubber boots, just standing there looking at a puddle that had formed over his prized azaleas. 

It made me think of when I was a kid. We used to love the rain. My brother and I would put on our galoshes—do people still call them galoshes? Anyway, we'd go out and try to build dams in the gutters with mud and sticks. We'd get absolutely filthy, and my mother would make us strip down to our underwear on the back porch before she'd let us in the house. She had this old galvanized steel bucket she kept out there just for our muddy clothes. 

But yeah, to get back to what you asked, I haven't ever been depressed for weeks at a time. I'm usually pretty even-keeled.
Have you ever had a time in your life when you felt down or lost interest in things for a period of two weeks or more, even if it wasn't recent?

Felt down or lost interest for two weeks or more? Like, in my whole life? No, I don't think so. I mean, I've had rough patches, sure, but nothing that lasted that long or made me lose interest in my life. 

Though, speaking of losing interest, did you hear they're canceling that sci-fi show on Channel 8? The one with the time-traveling detectives? I am so annoyed. I've been watching it since season one. They always do this, right? They get you hooked on a great storyline, build up all this suspense, and then right when they're about to reveal who the mole in the agency is, bam. Canceled. The network executives always say it's about ratings, but I read an article online—on one of those entertainment blogs, you know the ones with all the pop-up ads for car insurance—that said it was actually a dispute over the production budget. 

Apparently, the lead actor, the guy who plays Detective Vance, he wanted a massive trailer. Like, a two-story thing with a full kitchen and a hot tub. Can you imagine? A hot tub on a television set. It reminds me of this guy I used to work with, Gary. Gary was a piece of work. He insisted on having this ergonomic, zero-gravity chair at his desk. It looked like something out of a spaceship. He said it was for his lumbar support, but he'd recline it all the way back during conference calls and practically fall asleep. We had this one meeting with the VP of Operations, and Gary is just snoring softly in the corner, looking like an astronaut ready for liftoff. 

But anyway, no. I haven't had any long stretches like that where I felt down or stopped caring about things.
Have you ever had a period in your life lasting at least two weeks where you felt down, lost interest in things, or had trouble enjoying activities you usually liked?

Well... I know I just kept saying no to that, but... I guess if I'm being completely honest, that is actually what finally made me agree to come in here. I just don't care about the things that used to keep me balanced. My sailing races, my Saturday historical society shift, even just tinkering out in the woodshop... they all just feel like chores I keep putting off. 

Especially the historical society. I used to love going down there on weekends. We've been working on archiving these old city planning maps from the 1920s, and it's fascinating stuff, really. You can actually see where the original trolley lines were supposed to go before they all got torn up. My buddy Frank—he's the head archivist down there, guy wears a bowtie every single day, I kid you not—he found this original blueprint for a suspension bridge they were going to build over the gorge. It never got funded, obviously, because of the Great Depression. 

Speaking of the Depression, my grandmother used to save aluminum foil because of how she grew up back then. She'd wash it out, smooth it completely flat, and fold it up in this little drawer by her sink. I opened that drawer after she passed away, and there must have been five hundred perfectly folded, shiny little squares of Reynolds Wrap in there. It's funny the habits people hold onto, isn't it? 

But, yeah... I just haven't been going to my shifts. Or out to the woodshop. It all just feels like too much effort lately.
Have you ever had a period in your life before this one where you felt down, lost interest in things, or had trouble enjoying activities you usually liked for at least two weeks in a row?

Before this current slump? No, honestly, I've never had anything like this happen before. I've always been the guy keeping everything on track, you know? It's kind of my job. 

Actually, speaking of keeping things on track, it reminds me of this massive software migration I managed back in 2014. We were switching the whole company over to a new CRM system, and my boss at the time—this woman named Brenda, absolute micromanager—she insisted we do the entire cutover during a holiday weekend. Thanksgiving weekend, if you can believe it. Who does a major IT rollout on Thanksgiving? 

I ended up missing my sister's famous deep-fried turkey that year. Have you ever had deep-fried turkey? It's incredible, the skin gets so crispy, but it is incredibly dangerous to make. My brother-in-law, Dave, he actually almost burned down his detached garage one year because he didn't thaw the bird completely before dropping it in. The ice hits that boiling peanut oil and it just erupts like a volcano. He singed his eyebrows clean off and had to replace the vinyl siding on half the garage. His homeowner's insurance actually dropped him after that. He had to go with this cut-rate policy that barely covers anything, and the deductibles are through the roof. 

But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, feeling down before this. No, this is definitely a first for me. I've never lost my drive or felt like this in the past.

Have you ever had a time in your life before this current period where you experienced a major depressive episode—meaning you felt down or lost interest in things nearly every day for at least two weeks in a row?

Before this? No, I really haven't. Like I said, this whole... feeling like everything is just too much effort, it's completely new territory for me. I've always been the one driving things forward. 

You know, speaking of driving things forward, I actually bought a vintage Mustang a few years ago. A '67 fastback. Beautiful car, cherry red. I spent two whole summers restoring the engine block. I had to source these original carburetor parts from this guy out in Arizona who runs a salvage yard specifically for classic Fords. He was quite a character, actually. He'd only communicate by fax. Can you imagine? In this day and age, firing up a fax machine just to order a distributor cap. 

It made me think about how much technology has changed. When I first started in project management, we were still using physical whiteboards and sticky notes for everything. Now it's all Jira boards and Slack channels. My nephew, he just started an internship at a tech startup, and he told me they don't even have set working hours. They just have to "deliver results." I asked him what happens if he needs to reach someone at 9 AM and they're asleep, and he just shrugged and said he'd send a Slack message. It's a whole different world. 

But yeah, to answer your question, no. I've never had a time like this before where I just didn't care about anything for weeks on end. It's just this one time, recently.
Have you ever had a time in your life before this current period where you felt down or lost interest in things nearly every day for at least two weeks in a row?

I feel like I'm repeating myself a bit, Doc. Did I not explain that right earlier? But no, honestly, never before this current stretch. I've always been completely fine, very steady. 

Actually, speaking of steady, I had this guy come out to look at my back deck a while ago because the railing was feeling a little wobbly. Turns out the support posts were completely rotted out at the bottom. The contractor told me that the pressure-treated lumber they sell these days just doesn't hold up like the old stuff used to. Back in the day, they used to treat wood with this chemical called CCA—chromated copper arsenate, I think. They banned it for residential use back in the early 2000s because of the arsenic in it. Which, you know, obviously makes sense. You don't want kids playing around arsenic. 

My daughter, when she was little, she used to basically live on that deck during the summer. She had this massive collection of those plastic Barbie cars and playsets, and she would set up an entire sprawling city out there. We had to put a huge patio umbrella over it so the plastic wouldn't melt in the August heat. I actually remember buying that umbrella at a Sears that was going out of business. Man, it's wild how all those big anchor department stores just completely vanished, isn't it? You walk into a mall these days and it's basically a ghost town. Just a pretzel stand and a bunch of empty storefronts. 

But anyway, sorry, what were we saying? Right, feeling down. No, never before this. Just this one time, recently.
Have you ever had a time in your life before this current period where you felt down or lost interest in things nearly every day for at least two weeks in a row?

Doc, are you messing with me? I feel like we're stuck in a loop here. I swear I just answered this, didn't I? But no, to be absolutely clear, I have never felt like this before in my life. Never had a two-week stretch of feeling down or losing interest before this recent stuff. 

But you know, speaking of loops and repeating things, it totally reminds me of this massive compliance audit we had to do at work a few years back. The external auditors kept asking us for the exact same expense reports, over and over, just worded slightly differently on their forms. It drove my accounting lead absolutely up the wall. We had this one guy, Gary, who got so frustrated he actually brought in a stress ball shaped like a giant tomato, and he squeezed it so hard one afternoon that it literally popped. Got this weird, sticky foam stuff all over his expensive mechanical keyboard. He had to use a whole can of that compressed air to blow it out from under the keys. 

You know those compressed air dusters? They actually get freezing cold if you hold the trigger down too long. It's an endothermic reaction. I learned that from my high school chemistry teacher, Mr. Henderson. He used to wear these ridiculous polka-dot bowties every single day. I don't think I ever saw the man in a regular necktie. 

Anyway, I'm rambling again, sorry. But yeah, to be totally clear: no. Never felt down like this before.
Have you ever had a time in your life before this current period where you felt down or lost interest in things nearly every day for at least two weeks in a row?

Okay, seriously, Doc, is this a test? Like, a memory test? Because I'm starting to feel like I'm taking crazy pills here. I've told you, like, three times now. No. I have never, ever had a time before this current situation where I felt this down or lost interest in things for two weeks. Never. 

It's actually kind of funny, you asking the same thing over and over. It reminds me of my dog, Buster. He's a golden retriever mix, and I swear, his memory resets every time I walk out the front door. I can go out to grab the mail, be gone for thirty seconds, and when I come back in, he acts like I've been deployed overseas for a year. He does this little tippy-tap dance on the hardwood floors, and his nails click-clack so loudly. I actually had to put down a runner rug in the hallway because he was scratching up the finish. 

Getting the floors refinished was a nightmare, by the way. The dust gets everywhere. You think you've sealed off the rooms with plastic sheeting, but somehow, that fine sawdust just permeates the entire house. I was finding it in my cereal bowls a week later. The guy who did the floors, his name was Sal, he told me he uses a special HEPA filter vacuum, but I think he was full of it. He also tried to talk me into a darker stain, like an espresso color, but I told him, no way, that just shows every speck of dirt. 

But yeah, anyway... no. Never been depressed like this before. Just this once. Can we move on to the next question now?
Before this current period you're describing, have you ever had a time in your life where you felt down or lost interest in things nearly every day for at least two weeks in a row?

Doc, I... I really don't know what to say. Are we... is there a hidden camera in here? Because I'm honestly starting to feel a little frustrated. I've said it, I don't know how many times now. No. Never. Before this current thing, I have never felt down or lost interest in things for two weeks. I've always been completely fine. 

You asking me the same exact thing four times in a row, it's... it's honestly making me think of this telemarketer who used to call my house. Same time, every Tuesday evening, right when we were sitting down for dinner. Always trying to sell me some extended warranty on a car I hadn't owned in a decade. I'd tell him, "Buddy, I sold that Honda Civic in 2012," and he'd just read right off his script again. 

I actually really loved that Civic, though. It was a manual transmission. You just don't see stick shifts anymore, do you? Everyone wants automatics, or those electric cars where you don't even feel the gears shifting. My neighbor just bought one of those Teslas, and the thing is completely silent. It's actually kind of dangerous. He almost backed into my garbage cans last week because I didn't even hear him pulling out of his driveway. 

Speaking of garbage cans, the city just switched to these new automated trucks where the mechanical arm comes out and grabs the bin. But half the time, the driver misses and knocks the can over, and there's trash all over the street. I had to go out there with a broom on Tuesday and sweep up half a box of packing peanuts that blew into my azalea bushes. 

Anyway... look, I'm sorry, but no. Never before this. Can we please talk about something else?
Before this current period, have you ever had a time when you felt down or lost interest in things nearly every day for at least two weeks?

Okay, I... I honestly don't know what's happening right now. Are you reading the wrong line on your screen? Is your computer frozen? Because I am answering this for the fifth time now. No. Absolutely not. Never in my entire life before this current mess have I felt down or lost interest for two weeks. 

It's like... it's like a software glitch. Are you glitching, Doc? Actually, we had this massive glitch when we migrated our project management tools over to a new cloud server last spring at work. Every time I'd close out a milestone on the Gantt chart, the system would just duplicate it. So I ended up with, like, twenty identical tasks for 'Phase 1 Review.' I had to get IT on the horn, and the guy they sent—this kid named Tyler—he spent three hours trying to fix it while chewing on these incredibly loud ice cubes from his iced coffee. 

Just crunch, crunch, crunch, right in my ear. I don't know how people can chew ice like that. Doesn't it hurt their teeth? My dentist told me chewing ice is the number one way people crack their molars. Dental crowns are not cheap, let me tell you. I had to get one last year on my back left tooth, and even with my insurance, it was an absolute fortune. And the mold they put in your mouth to size it? It tastes like stale peppermint and rubber. It made me gag so hard the dental assistant had to turn on a fan and point it right at my face. 

But, uh... look. I really don't know how else to say it. No. Never had a two-week period like that before this. Please, I'm begging you, can we move on to the next question?
